---
title: "Glossary of IRT terms"
description: >
  Plain-language definitions of the terms used in item response theory, each
  with the mirtverse or mirt function that computes it, and pictures where a
  picture helps.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE,
                      echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.2,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "85%", dpi = 110)
```

```{r setup, eval = TRUE, include = FALSE}
library(mirtverse)
library(ggplot2)
cols <- c("#2C5F8A", "#D1495B", "#2E8B57", "#E09F3E", "#7A7A7A")
theta <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 201)
p3 <- function(theta, a = 1, b = 0, g = 0, u = 1)
  g + (u - g) / (1 + exp(-a * (theta - b)))
curves <- function(pars) {
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pars)), function(i)
    data.frame(theta = theta, p = p3(theta, pars$a[i], pars$b[i], pars$g[i]),
               item = pars$label[i])))
  out$item <- factor(out$item, levels = unique(pars$label))  # keep legend order
  out
}
base_plot <- function(df, ylab = "P(correct)") {
  ggplot(df, aes(theta, p, colour = item)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = expression(theta ~ "(ability)"), y = ylab) +
    theme_mirtverse()
}
lsat <- mirt(expand.table(LSAT7), 1, verbose = FALSE)
sci <- mirt(Science, 1, verbose = FALSE)
```

This page explains the words you will meet in item response theory (IRT)
courses, papers and mirtverse output. Each entry gives a plain-language
definition, then **In R**: The mirtverse or mirt function that computes or
shows it. Function names link to their help pages.

The entries are grouped in the order a course usually meets them, from the
basic ideas to test design. Use the A to Z index below to jump to a term, or
your browser's search (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F) to find a word.

To try the code, load the package and fit a model to one of the example
datasets that come with mirt:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
library(mirtverse)
mod <- mirt(expand.table(LSAT7), 1)   # five 0/1 items, 2PL model
```

## The basic ideas {#basics}

### Item response theory {#item-response-theory}

A family of statistical models that link a person's answers to test items
with an unobserved trait, such as math ability or anxiety. Each item gets its
own parameters (how hard it is, how well it separates people), so the model
can say how likely any person is to give any answer. Unlike a sum score, an
IRT score accounts for *which* items a person answered correctly, and its
precision can be stated at every level of the trait.

**In R:** `mirt::mirt()` fits the model; `tidy()` lists the item parameters
and `interpret()` describes the results in sentences.

### Latent trait (theta) {#latent-trait}

The characteristic a test is meant to measure but that cannot be observed
directly, such as reading ability. It is written with the Greek letter theta
(θ). Theta is usually scaled so that the group the test was calibrated on has
a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, so θ = 1 means "one standard
deviation above the average test taker".

**In R:** `fscores()` estimates each person's theta; `augment()` adds the
estimates to your data.

### Ability {#ability}

The everyday name for the latent trait in achievement tests. On a survey the
same quantity might be called an attitude or a symptom level; the mathematics
is the same.

### Logit {#logit}

The unit of the theta scale in logistic IRT models. A logit is the logarithm
of the odds of a correct answer. A one-logit gap between a person's ability
and an item's difficulty changes the odds of success by a factor of about
2.7, whatever the starting point.

### Item {#item}

One question, task or statement on a test or questionnaire. In R each item
is one column of the response data, and each row is one person.

**In R:** `profile_data()` summarises the columns of a dataset;
`mirt::key2binary()` turns multiple-choice answers into 0/1 scores.

### Dichotomous item {#dichotomous-item}

An item scored in two categories, usually 0 (wrong) and 1 (right). True/false
and scored multiple-choice items are dichotomous.

### Polytomous item {#polytomous-item}

An item with more than two ordered score categories, such as a rating scale
(strongly disagree to strongly agree) or an essay scored 0 to 4.

**In R:** Fit with `itemtype = "graded"` or `"gpcm"` in `mirt::mirt()`.

### Sum score {#sum-score}

The number of points a person earns, added up over the items (also called the
raw or number-correct score). It is easy to explain but treats every item as
equally important and gives no item-by-item view of precision.

**In R:** `rowSums(data)`; `mirt::itemstats()` reports the sum-score
distribution.

### Classical test theory {#classical-test-theory}

The older framework that IRT builds on. It describes a test with sum-score
statistics such as item p-values, item-total correlations and coefficient
alpha. These statistics depend on the group that took the test, while IRT
item parameters (once on a common scale) do not.

**In R:** `mirt::itemstats()`; `item_table()` shows classical and IRT
statistics side by side.

### Item p-value (classical difficulty) {#p-value}

The proportion of people who answered an item correctly (or the mean item
score for polytomous items). Despite the name, a *high* p-value means an
*easy* item. It is not the same as the p-value of a significance test.

**In R:** The `mean` column of `item_table()`.

### Item-total correlation {#item-total-correlation}

The correlation between an item score and the sum of the other items. It is
the classical index of discrimination: Low or negative values (below about
0.2) suggest a miskeyed, confusing or off-topic item.

**In R:** The `item_total_r` column of `item_table()`.

### Dimensionality and unidimensionality {#dimensionality}

The number of distinct traits a test measures. Most IRT models used in
practice are *unidimensional*: They assume one trait explains how people
answer. If a math test also measures reading speed, a one-dimensional model
may misfit.

**In R:** Compare `mirt(data, 1)` with `mirt(data, 2)` using `anova()`;
`select_model()` can include a two-factor candidate with `dims = 1:2`.

### Local independence {#local-independence}

The assumption that, for people at the same theta, answers to different
items are unrelated: Once ability is known, getting item 3 right tells you
nothing more about item 4. It is what lets the model multiply item
probabilities together. See [local dependence](#local-dependence) for how it
fails.

## Models {#models}

### Rasch model (1PL) {#rasch-model}

The simplest IRT model for 0/1 items. Each item has only a difficulty; all
items are assumed to discriminate equally. Under the Rasch model the sum score
contains all the information about ability, which is why it is popular for
tests that must be scored by hand. The one-parameter logistic (1PL) model is
the same model with the common discrimination estimated rather than fixed
at 1.

**In R:** `mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "Rasch")`.

### Two-parameter logistic model (2PL) {#two-pl}

Adds a [discrimination](#discrimination) parameter to each item, so some items
can separate people more sharply than others. The probability of a correct
answer is

$$P(\theta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-a(\theta - b)}}$$

where *a* is the discrimination and *b* the difficulty.

**In R:** `mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "2PL")` (the default for 0/1 items).

### Three-parameter logistic model (3PL) {#three-pl}

Adds a [lower asymptote](#guessing) *g* (often called *c*) for multiple-choice
items, where even very low-ability test takers can guess right:

$$P(\theta) = g + \frac{1 - g}{1 + e^{-a(\theta - b)}}$$

The 3PL needs large samples to estimate well; with fewer than about 1,000
people the guessing parameters are often unstable.

**In R:** `mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "3PL")`. `select_model()` compares the
Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models for you and explains its choice.

### Graded response model {#graded-response-model}

A model for ordered polytomous items, such as rating scales. It models the
probability of scoring *in or above* each category with a 2PL-like curve, so
an item with *k* categories has one discrimination and *k* − 1
[thresholds](#threshold).

**In R:** `mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "graded")`.

### Generalized partial credit model (GPCM) {#gpcm}

Another model for ordered categories. It models each step from one category
to the next (from 1 to 2, from 2 to 3) separately. Its step parameters can be
out of order, which can reveal a category that is rarely the most likely
response. The partial credit model is its Rasch version.

**In R:** `mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "gpcm")` or `itemtype = "Rasch"` for
polytomous data.

### Multidimensional IRT {#multidimensional-irt}

Models with two or more latent traits, each item loading on one or several of
them. They are used when a test deliberately measures several skills, or to
check whether a single trait is enough.

**In R:** `mirt(data, 2)` for an exploratory two-factor model, or a
`mirt::mirt.model()` specification for a confirmatory structure.

## Item parameters and curves {#item-parameters-and-curves}

### Item parameters {#item-parameters}

The numbers that describe how an item behaves: Discrimination, difficulty and,
in some models, guessing and an upper asymptote. They are estimated once,
during [calibration](#calibration), and then reused to score anyone who takes
the item.

**In R:** `tidy()` returns one row per parameter; `coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE,
simplify = TRUE)` is the mirt equivalent.

### Item characteristic curve (ICC) {#item-characteristic-curve}

The S-shaped curve that shows the probability of a correct answer at every
level of theta. It is also called a trace line. The steepness of the curve is
the [discrimination](#discrimination); its location is the
[difficulty](#difficulty).

```{r icc, eval = TRUE, fig.alt = "Three item characteristic curves: an easy item to the left, a medium item in the middle, and a hard item to the right."}
base_plot(curves(data.frame(a = 1.2, b = c(-1.5, 0, 1.5), g = 0,
                            label = c("easy (b = -1.5)", "medium (b = 0)",
                                      "hard (b = 1.5)")))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50")
```

**In R:** `gg_trace(mod)`; `mirt::itemplot()` for one item.

### Difficulty (location, *b*) {#difficulty}

The point on the theta scale where the item characteristic curve crosses a
50% chance of success (for the 2PL and Rasch models). An item with *b* = 1 is
answered correctly by half the people whose ability is one standard deviation
above average. Higher *b* means a harder item. For polytomous items the
location is usually the mean of the [thresholds](#threshold).

**In R:** The `b` rows of `tidy()`, or the `location` column of
`item_table()`.

### Discrimination (slope, *a*) {#discrimination}

How steeply the item characteristic curve rises: How sharply the item
separates people just below its difficulty from people just above it.
Values around 1 to 2 are typical. Values below about 0.5 mean the item tells
you little about ability; negative values usually mean a miskeyed item.

```{r discrimination, eval = TRUE, fig.alt = "Two curves with the same difficulty: a steep curve with high discrimination and a flat curve with low discrimination."}
base_plot(curves(data.frame(a = c(2.5, 0.5), b = 0, g = 0,
                            label = c("high (a = 2.5)", "low (a = 0.5)"))))
```

**In R:** The `a` rows of `tidy()`, or the `discrimination` column of
`item_table()`, which flags low values.

### Guessing (lower asymptote, *c* or *g*) {#guessing}

The chance that a person with very low ability still answers correctly, the
height of the curve's left tail. For a four-option multiple-choice item it
is often near 0.20 to 0.25. Only the 3PL and 4PL models estimate it.

```{r guessing, eval = TRUE, fig.alt = "A 3PL curve that levels off at 0.2 on the left, compared with a 2PL curve that goes down to zero."}
base_plot(curves(data.frame(a = 1.5, b = 0, g = c(0, 0.2),
                            label = c("no guessing (g = 0)", "3PL (g = 0.2)")))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.2, linetype = "dotted", colour = cols[2])
```

**In R:** The `g` rows of `tidy()` for a 3PL model.

### Upper asymptote (*u*) {#upper-asymptote}

The highest probability of success, even for very able people. It is 1 in most
models; the four-parameter (4PL) model estimates it, for example when able
test takers sometimes slip on an item.

**In R:** `itemtype = "4PL"`; the `u` rows of `tidy()`.

### Slope-intercept form {#slope-intercept}

The way mirt stores parameters internally: The 2PL is written as
1 / (1 + exp(−(*a*θ + *d*))), where *d* is an intercept, rather than with the
difficulty *b*. The two are related by *b* = −*d* / *a*. Multidimensional
models are always reported this way, because one difficulty no longer makes
sense.

**In R:** `coef(mod)` gives slope-intercept values, `coef(mod, IRTpars =
TRUE)` the traditional ones; `tidy(mod, IRTpars = FALSE)` does the same.

### Threshold {#threshold}

For a polytomous item, the point on the theta scale where a person becomes
more likely to score in a higher category than in the one below (GPCM), or
has a 50% chance of scoring in or above a category (graded model). An item
with five categories has four thresholds.

**In R:** The `b1`, `b2`, … rows of `tidy()`.

### Category response curve {#category-response-curve}

For a polytomous item, one curve per score category showing how likely each
category is at every theta. Low categories dominate on the left, high ones on
the right. A category that is never the most likely anywhere may be
redundant.

```{r category-curves, eval = TRUE, fig.alt = "Category response curves for a four-category item from the Science data: each category is most likely over a different range of theta."}
gg_trace(sci, which.items = 1)
```

**In R:** `gg_trace(mod)` for polytomous items (shown above for the first
item of the `Science` data).

### Expected score {#expected-score}

The average score a person at a given theta would get on an item: The
probability of success for a 0/1 item, or the probability-weighted average
category for a polytomous one. Summed over items it gives the
[test characteristic curve](#test-characteristic-curve).

**In R:** `mirt::expected.item()`; `gg_trace(mod, type = "expected")`.

### Test characteristic curve (TCC) {#test-characteristic-curve}

The expected sum score at every level of theta, found by adding up the item
curves. It converts between the theta scale and the sum-score scale, and is
the basis of [characteristic-curve linking](#characteristic-curve-linking).

**In R:** `mirt::expected.test()`; `plot(mod, type = "score")`.

## Estimating the model and scoring people {#estimation-and-scoring}

### Calibration {#calibration}

Estimating the item parameters from a sample of responses. A calibration
sample should be large enough for the model (a few hundred people for the
Rasch model, 500 or more for the 2PL, often 1,000 or more for the 3PL) and
similar to the people who will take the test.

**In R:** `mirt::mirt()`; in a pipeline, `calibrate()`.

### Marginal maximum likelihood and the EM algorithm {#marginal-maximum-likelihood}

The standard way of estimating item parameters. It finds the item parameters
that make the observed responses most likely, averaging over the unknown
abilities instead of estimating them at the same time. The EM
(expectation-maximization) algorithm does this in cycles until the estimates
stop changing.

**In R:** The default `method = "EM"` in `mirt::mirt()`.

### Convergence {#convergence}

Whether the estimation algorithm reached a stable solution. A model that has
not converged should not be used: Try more cycles (`technical = list(NCYCLES
= 2000)`), a simpler model or better starting values.

**In R:** The `converged` column of `glance()`; `extract.mirt(mod,
"converged")`.

### Standard error (of a parameter) {#standard-error}

How uncertain an estimated item parameter is. Small samples, extreme items and
complex models give large standard errors.

**In R:** Fit with `SE = TRUE`, then `tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE)` adds the
standard errors and confidence limits.

### Person score (ability estimate) {#person-score}

An estimate of a person's theta from their answers and the item parameters.
mirt calls these factor scores. The main methods differ mostly for people
with very high, very low or very short response patterns.

**In R:** `fscores(mod, method = "EAP")`; `augment()` adds scores and their
standard errors to the data; `score_persons()` does it in a pipeline;
`gg_scores()` plots their distribution.

### EAP (expected a posteriori) {#eap}

The average of the possible theta values, weighted by how well each fits the
person's answers and by a prior distribution (usually standard normal). It
always gives a finite score, even for all-correct patterns, but pulls scores
slightly toward the mean. It is mirt's default.

**In R:** `fscores(mod, method = "EAP")`.

### MAP (maximum a posteriori) {#map}

The single most likely theta once the prior is taken into account. Similar to
EAP, with a little more pull toward the mean.

**In R:** `fscores(mod, method = "MAP")`.

### Maximum likelihood (ML) scoring {#ml-scoring}

The theta that makes the person's answers most likely, without a prior. It is
unbiased for long tests but gives infinite scores for all-correct or
all-wrong patterns.

**In R:** `fscores(mod, method = "ML")`.

### WLE (weighted likelihood estimate) {#wle}

A version of ML scoring with a correction that reduces its bias on short tests
and gives finite scores for perfect patterns. Common in large-scale
assessments and Rasch work.

**In R:** `fscores(mod, method = "WLE")`.

## Precision and targeting {#precision}

### Item information {#item-information}

How much an item reduces uncertainty about theta at each ability level. An
item is most informative near its difficulty, and more discriminating items
give more information. Information is what makes items "work" for some
people and not others: A hard item tells you a lot about strong students and
almost nothing about weak ones.

**In R:** `gg_info(mod, type = "items")`; `mirt::iteminfo()`.

### Test information {#test-information}

The sum of the item informations: How precisely the whole test measures at
each theta. A test built to make pass/fail decisions should have its peak
near the [cut score](#cut-score).

### Standard error of measurement (conditional SEM) {#standard-error-of-measurement}

How far a person's estimated theta is likely to be from their true theta. In
IRT it depends on theta: SEM = 1 / √(test information), so it is smallest
where the test has the most information. A standard error of 0.3 means a
95% interval of about ±0.6 around the estimate.

```{r info, eval = TRUE, fig.alt = "Test information for the LSAT7 data, peaking below average ability, with the standard error of measurement rising toward the high end of the scale."}
gg_info(lsat)
```

**In R:** `gg_info(mod)` shows information and SEM together (above, for the
`LSAT7` data); `gg_info(mod, type = "se")` shows the SEM alone. The
standard errors of individual scores come from `fscores(mod,
full.scores.SE = TRUE)` or `augment()`.

### Marginal reliability {#marginal-reliability}

A single summary of precision for a whole population, on the familiar 0-to-1
reliability scale: The share of the variance in theta estimates that is true
differences between people rather than measurement error. Above 0.90 is
excellent, 0.80 good and 0.70 acceptable for most uses.

**In R:** The `reliability` column of `glance()`; `mirt::marginal_rxx()`;
`mirt::empirical_rxx()` for reliability of the estimated scores.

### Targeting {#targeting}

How well the difficulty of the items matches the ability of the people. A
well-targeted test has items spread where the people are. A test that is too
easy gives little information about the strongest test takers.

**In R:** `gg_wright()`; `interpret()` comments on targeting.

### Wright map {#wright-map}

A picture that places people (as a histogram) and items (as points) on the
same theta scale, so you can see targeting at a glance. Named after Benjamin
Wright, who popularised it for Rasch measurement.

```{r wright, eval = TRUE, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Wright map for the LSAT7 data: the person distribution on the left and the five item locations on the right, mostly below average ability."}
gg_wright(lsat)
```

**In R:** `gg_wright(mod)`.

## Checking the model {#checking-fit}

### Model fit {#model-fit}

How well the model as a whole reproduces the data. In IRT it is usually
judged with limited-information statistics such as [M2](#m2) and the indices
derived from it. Poor fit can come from the wrong model, more than one
dimension, or a few bad items.

**In R:** `glance()` reports M2, RMSEA, SRMSR, CFI and TLI in one row;
`mirt::M2()` gives the details.

### M2 {#m2}

A chi-square test of model fit based on the pairs of items (how often each
pair is answered correctly together). With large samples it almost always
rejects, so the effect-size indices below matter more. For polytomous items
mirtverse uses the related C2 statistic.

**In R:** The `M2`, `df` and `p.value` columns of `glance()`.

### RMSEA {#rmsea}

Root mean square error of approximation: Misfit per degree of freedom, where
0 is perfect. Common guidelines are below 0.05 for close fit and below 0.08
for reasonable fit. The same index is reported for each item from the
[S-X2](#s-x2) statistic.

**In R:** The `RMSEA` column of `glance()` (model) and of `item_table()`
(items).

### SRMSR {#srmsr}

Standardized root mean square residual: The average difference between the
observed and model-implied correlations between items. Values below about
0.05 indicate good fit.

**In R:** The `SRMSR` column of `glance()`.

### CFI and TLI {#cfi-tli}

Comparative fit indices that compare the model with a baseline in which the
items are unrelated. Values of 0.95 or above are usually taken as good fit.

**In R:** The `CFI` and `TLI` columns of `glance()`.

### Information criteria (AIC, BIC, SABIC) {#information-criteria}

Numbers for comparing models fitted to the same data: They reward fit and
penalise extra parameters. *Smaller is better*. BIC penalises complexity more
than AIC and tends to choose simpler models; SABIC is in between.

**In R:** The `AIC`, `BIC` and `SABIC` columns of `glance()`;
`select_model()` uses BIC by default; `anova(mod1, mod2)`.

### Likelihood-ratio test {#likelihood-ratio-test}

A significance test comparing two *nested* models, where one is a special
case of the other (the Rasch model is a 2PL with equal slopes). A small
p-value means the more complex model fits significantly better.

**In R:** `anova(mod_rasch, mod_2pl)`; the `lrt` element of
`select_model()`.

### Item fit {#item-fit}

Whether each item behaves the way the model predicts. A misfitting item may
be poorly written, miskeyed, or measuring something else.

**In R:** `item_table()` (with a `flag` column), `gg_itemfit()`,
`mirt::itemfit()`; `item_card()` for one item in depth.

### S-X2 {#s-x2}

The most widely used item-fit statistic for IRT (Orlando and Thissen). It
groups people by sum score and compares the observed proportion correct in
each group with the model's prediction. A small p-value signals misfit; with
many items, adjust the p-values for multiple testing.

**In R:** The `S_X2`, `p.value` and `RMSEA` columns of `item_table()`;
`gg_itemfit()` plots them.

### Empirical item curve {#empirical-item-curve}

The observed proportion correct in groups of people with similar ability,
plotted over the model's curve. When the dots follow the line, the item fits.

**In R:** `gg_empirical(mod, item = 1)`; `mirt::itemfit(mod, empirical.plot
= 1)`.

### Local dependence {#local-dependence}

When two items are related beyond what the trait explains, breaking
[local independence](#local-independence). Common causes are items that share
a reading passage, items where one answer gives away another, or near-duplicate
wording. It makes the test look more reliable than it is.

**In R:** `gg_q3()`; `residuals(mod, type = "Q3")`.

### Q3 {#q3}

Yen's Q3 statistic: The correlation between two items' residuals (observed
minus expected score) after the trait is taken out. Pairs whose Q3 is more
than 0.2 above the average Q3 are worth a look.

**In R:** `gg_q3(mod)` draws a heatmap and marks the flagged pairs.

### Person fit {#person-fit}

Whether a person's pattern of answers is consistent with the model, for
example a person who misses easy items but gets hard ones right. Misfit can
mean guessing, cheating, carelessness or a scoring error.

**In R:** `mirt::personfit()`; `interpret()` reports the share of people
flagged.

### Zh (or lz) {#zh}

The usual person-fit statistic: A standardized log-likelihood of the person's
answers. Large negative values (below −1.96) flag unusual patterns.

**In R:** The `Zh` column of `mirt::personfit(mod)`.

## Fairness {#fairness}

### Differential item functioning (DIF) {#dif}

An item has DIF when people from different groups who have the *same* ability
have different chances of answering it correctly. DIF is not the same as a
group difference in average scores: Groups can truly differ in ability. DIF
means the item itself behaves differently, for example because of a word that
is harder in translation.

**In R:** `dif(data, group = "language")` tests every item and reports
effect sizes; `gg_dif()` plots them; `mirt::DIF()` gives more control.

### Reference and focal groups {#reference-focal-group}

In a DIF study, the reference group is the comparison group (often the
majority) and the focal group is the one whose fairness is in question.

**In R:** The `reference` and `focal` elements of `dif()`.

### Uniform and non-uniform DIF {#uniform-nonuniform-dif}

With *uniform* DIF the item is harder for one group at every ability level
(the curves are shifted). With *non-uniform* DIF the gap changes with ability
and the curves can cross, so the item favours one group at low ability and
the other at high ability.

```{r dif, eval = TRUE, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Two panels: uniform DIF, where the focal group's curve is shifted right of the reference group's curve; and non-uniform DIF, where the two curves cross."}
dif_df <- rbind(
  transform(curves(data.frame(a = 1.3, b = c(-0.3, 0.4), g = 0,
                              label = c("reference", "focal"))),
            type = "Uniform DIF"),
  transform(curves(data.frame(a = c(1.8, 0.7), b = 0, g = 0,
                              label = c("reference", "focal"))),
            type = "Non-uniform DIF"))
dif_df$type <- factor(dif_df$type, c("Uniform DIF", "Non-uniform DIF"))
base_plot(dif_df) + facet_wrap(~type)
```

**In R:** `dif()` tests all the item parameters by default, so it finds both
kinds; the `uesd` effect size captures crossing curves.

### DIF effect size {#dif-effect-size}

How big the DIF is, in score units, rather than just whether it is
statistically significant. mirtverse reports the expected score difference
between focal and reference group at the same ability, averaged over the
focal group: `esd` is signed (positive means the item favours the focal
group) and `uesd` unsigned. For 0/1 items these are differences in
probability, so 0.05 means five percentage points.

**In R:** The `esd` and `uesd` columns of `dif()`.

### Anchor items {#anchor-items}

Items assumed to be free of DIF (in a DIF study) or shared by two forms (in
[linking](#linking)). They hold the scale in place while other items are
compared.

**In R:** The `items` argument of `dif()` (untested items act as anchors);
`link_to_bank()` finds the anchors shared with a bank.

## Scales, linking and item banks {#linking-section}

### Linking and equating {#linking}

Putting results from different test forms or administrations on the same
theta scale. Each calibration sets its own zero point (the mean of its
sample), so parameters from two calibrations cannot be compared until they
are linked through common [anchor items](#anchor-items) or common people.
Equating is linking strict enough that scores on the forms can be used
interchangeably.

**In R:** `link_to_bank()`; `mirt::multipleGroup()` for concurrent
calibration.

### Characteristic-curve linking (Stocking-Lord and Haebara) {#characteristic-curve-linking}

Methods that find the linear transformation (θ on the bank scale = A × θ + B)
that makes the anchor items' curves from the new calibration match their bank
curves. Stocking-Lord matches the [test characteristic
curve](#test-characteristic-curve); Haebara matches each item curve.

**In R:** `link_to_bank(p, bank, method = "stocking-lord")` (the default) or
`method = "haebara"`.

### Mean-sigma and mean-mean linking {#moment-linking}

Simpler linking methods that set A and B from the means and standard
deviations of the anchor items' difficulties (mean-sigma) or the means of
their difficulties and discriminations (mean-mean).

**In R:** `link_to_bank(p, bank, method = "mean-sigma")`.

### Item bank {#item-bank}

A collection of calibrated items on one common scale, with their parameters,
content codes and history, from which tests are built.

**In R:** `mv_bank()` starts a bank, `bank_items()` adds items,
`monitor_bank()` checks its health over time and `retire_items()` takes
items out.

### Parameter drift {#parameter-drift}

When an item's parameters change over time, for example because it has
leaked or the curriculum has changed. Drifting items should not be used as
anchors.

**In R:** `check_security()` flags drift against the bank.

## Making decisions with scores {#decisions}

### Cut score {#cut-score}

The score that separates two decisions or performance levels, such as pass
and fail, or "basic" and "proficient". It can be set on the theta scale or on
the sum-score scale.

**In R:** `set_cuts()`.

### Standard setting (Bookmark and Angoff) {#standard-setting}

Structured procedures in which a panel of experts decides where cut scores
should be. In the *Bookmark* method panelists page through the items ordered
from easiest to hardest and place a bookmark where a just-qualified person
would stop succeeding. In the *Angoff* method panelists estimate, item by
item, the probability that a just-qualified person would answer correctly.

**In R:** `item_map()` builds the ordered item booklet for a Bookmark panel;
`set_cuts(p, panel = ratings)` turns the panel's ratings into cuts.

### Response probability (RP) {#response-probability}

The chance of success used to place items on the scale for a Bookmark
booklet. With RP67, each item is located where a person has a two-in-three
chance of answering correctly.

**In R:** The `rp` argument of `item_map()` (0.67 by default).

### Classification accuracy {#classification-accuracy}

The probability that a person is put in the category their *true* ability
belongs to. Errors are most likely for people near the cut, which is why a
test should be most precise there.

```{r accuracy, eval = TRUE, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Probability of passing as a function of true ability for a cut at theta = 0.5: it rises steeply around the cut, so people near the cut are the most likely to be misclassified."}
cut <- 0.5
sem <- 0.35
acc <- data.frame(theta = theta, p = pnorm((theta - cut) / sem), item = "P(pass)")
base_plot(acc, ylab = "P(observed pass)") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cut, linetype = "dashed", colour = cols[2]) +
  annotate("text", x = cut + 0.1, y = 0.08, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           label = "cut score", colour = cols[2]) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.9, y = 0.85, hjust = 0, size = 3,
           label = "Far from the cut,\ndecisions are almost\nalways right") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**In R:** `set_cuts()` reports it overall and by cut, with false positive
and false negative rates.

### Classification consistency {#classification-consistency}

The probability that two parallel administrations of the test would put a
person in the same category. A test can be consistent without being
accurate, but not the other way round.

**In R:** `set_cuts()`.

### Kappa {#kappa}

Cohen's kappa is agreement corrected for chance: 0 means no better than
chance, 1 means perfect agreement. It is reported with classification
consistency.

**In R:** `set_cuts()`.

## Building tests {#test-design}

### Automated test assembly {#automated-test-assembly}

Choosing items from a bank by optimisation so that a fixed form meets its
blueprint (so many algebra items, so many geometry items), keeps apart
*enemy items* that give each other away, and is as
informative as possible where it matters, such as at the cut score.

**In R:** `assemble_forms()`, with the blueprint from `set_blueprint()`.

### Parallel forms {#parallel-forms}

Two or more test forms with different items but nearly the same
[test information](#test-information) and content, so it should not matter
which one a person takes.

**In R:** `assemble_forms(p, n_forms = 2)` builds them and checks that their
information agrees.

### Computerized adaptive test (CAT) {#computerized-adaptive-test}

A test that picks each next item for the person taking it, usually the item
with the most information at their current ability estimate. CATs reach the
same precision as a fixed form with far fewer items, but need a large,
well-calibrated bank.

**In R:** `simulate_cat()` shows how long, precise and secure a CAT from your
bank would be; the mirtCAT package runs real ones.

### Multistage test (MST) {#multistage-test}

A test that adapts between blocks of items (modules) instead of after every
item: Everyone starts with the same routing module, then moves to an easier
or harder module depending on their score.

**In R:** `assemble_mst()`.

### Exposure {#exposure}

The share of test takers who see an item. Items with high exposure are more
likely to be shared or memorised. CATs need exposure control because the
best items would otherwise be given to everyone.

**In R:** `simulate_cat()` reports exposure (use `randomesque` to spread
it); `monitor_bank()` tracks it over time.

## Response times {#response-times}

### Time intensity {#time-intensity}

How long an item typically takes, on a log-seconds scale: The response-time
counterpart of difficulty. In van der Linden's lognormal model it is written
β (beta).

**In R:** `fit_rt()`; see the [response times
article](../articles/response-times.html).

### Speed {#speed}

A person's working pace, the response-time counterpart of ability (written
τ, tau). Speed and ability are separate traits, though they are often
correlated.

**In R:** `fit_rt()` estimates each person's speed and its correlation with
ability.

### Rapid guessing {#rapid-guessing}

Answering so quickly that the person cannot have read the item, a sign of low
effort. Rapid guesses are usually flagged with a time threshold, such as 10%
of the item's average time.

**In R:** `fit_rt(mod, rt, flag_method = "nt10")`.

### Response time effort (RTE) {#response-time-effort}

The share of a person's responses that are *not* rapid guesses. People with
low RTE (often below 0.90) may have scores that understate their ability.

**In R:** The `rte` column of `fit_rt()$persons`;
`autoplot(fit, type = "rte")` plots it.

## Open-ended responses and security {#open-ended-and-security}

### Quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) {#qwk}

Agreement between two raters (two humans, or a human and a machine) on an
ordered score scale. Disagreements count more the further apart the scores
are. Values of 0.70 or above are a common minimum for automated scoring.

**In R:** `score_open()` checks machine scores against human scores with
QWK before they are used.

### Preknowledge {#preknowledge}

When test takers have seen some items before the test, so they do much
better on those items than their ability on the others would predict.

**In R:** `check_security(p, leaked = c(...))`.

### Answer copying {#answer-copying}

Pairs of test takers who share many more identical *wrong* answers than their
scores would lead you to expect. A flag is evidence for an investigation, not
proof.

**In R:** `check_security()`.

## AI in measurement {#ai}

These terms come up when artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning
meet testing. The [AI Hub](ai-hub.html) collects mirtverse's AI material, and
the [translation table](ai-translation.html) maps many more machine learning
words to the psychometric ideas closest to them.

### Machine learning {#machine-learning}

Methods that learn a rule for predicting an outcome from data, judged by how
well they predict new cases rather than by whether their parameters mean
something. A logistic regression of item scores on ability is already a small
machine learning model; IRT adds the claim that the latent trait is what is
being measured.

**In R:** `score_open(p, responses, scorer = fit)` accepts any trained model
with a `predict()` method.

### Feature {#feature}

A measured property of a case that a model uses to predict something. For an
item, features might be its word count, readability or the number of steps it
takes; for an essay, its length or vocabulary. Features play the role that
covariates play in an explanatory IRT model.

### Overfitting and cross-validation {#cross-validation}

A model *overfits* when it learns the noise in its training data and predicts
new data worse than it predicted the old. *Cross-validation* estimates
accuracy honestly by fitting on part of the data and checking on the rest,
much as a calibration sample and a validation sample are kept apart.

### Embedding {#embedding}

A long vector of numbers that a language model uses to represent a word,
sentence or response, placed so that texts with similar meaning sit close
together. Embeddings can serve as features for scoring responses or
predicting item difficulty.

### Large language model (LLM) {#llm}

A neural network trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next
word, which lets it write, summarize, answer and score text when given
instructions. Claude and GPT are examples. Its output varies from run to run
and can be wrong, so every use in testing needs checks.

**In R:** `generate_items()`, `verify_items()`, `score_open()` and `mv_ask()`
can use an LLM set up with `mv_ask_setup()`.

### Prompt {#prompt}

The instructions and context given to a large language model, such as a
blueprint cell and an item-writing style guide, or a rubric and a student
response. Small changes in a prompt can change the output, so prompts are
part of the method and should be reported.

### Hallucination {#hallucination}

Fluent output from a language model that is false: An invented fact, a
wrong key, a citation that does not exist. In item writing it shows up as
items with no correct option or two correct options.

**In R:** `verify_items()` has a second model answer each item without the
key and flags disagreements.

### Human-in-the-loop {#human-in-the-loop}

A design in which people review, correct or approve what an AI system
produces before it counts, such as content experts reviewing generated items
or human raters scoring responses the engine is unsure about.

**In R:** `review_packet(p, ai_screen = TRUE)` and the low-confidence route
in `score_open()`.

### Automatic item generation (AIG) {#aig}

Producing many test items from a model of the item rather than writing each
one by hand. Classical AIG uses item models with variable parts; newer
approaches use language models. Either way, generated items still need
review and calibration.

**In R:** `generate_items()`.

### Item model {#item-model}

A template for a family of items: A parent item with elements that can vary
(numbers, names, contexts) and rules that keep each variant correct. Items
from one model are *isomorphs*, and often, but not always, have similar
difficulty.

**In R:** `item_model()`, `generate_isomorphs()` and `calibrate_families()`.

### Automated scoring {#automated-scoring}

Scoring constructed responses, such as essays or short answers, with a
computer model trained or instructed to match human raters. It is judged
against human scores with agreement statistics such as [QWK](#qwk) and
[PRMSE](#prmse), overall and within subgroups.

**In R:** `score_open()`.

### Differential scoring {#differential-scoring}

An automated scorer that gives one group of test takers lower (or higher)
scores than human raters give the same answers. It is checked by comparing
machine and human scores within groups, among responses that people scored
the same, so that bias in the scorer is not confused with a real
difference between the groups.

**In R:** `ai_audit()` with `group`.

### Validity argument {#validity-argument}

A structured case that test scores support their intended interpretation
and use (Kane, 2013). It links the claims (the scores follow the rubric,
generalize over occasions, reflect the construct, and support the
decisions made with them) to the evidence for each, and to the threats
against them. An AI component adds threats to every link.

**In R:** `validity_argument()`, with the evidence from `ai_audit()`.

### PRMSE {#prmse}

Proportional reduction in mean squared error: How much of the variance of
the *true* human score a machine score explains, after allowing for the
disagreement between human raters. Unlike agreement with one rater, it does
not penalize a machine for the noise in human scores.

### Linear logistic test model (LLTM) {#lltm}

A Rasch model in which each item's difficulty is a weighted sum of item
features, such as the cognitive operations the item needs. It is the
psychometric ancestor of predicting item difficulty from item text.

  decisions behind them on a realistic exam.

  workflow and what to read next.
